sources.original_text:
### Boiling (most reliable method)

- Bring the water to a **rolling boil (bubbling) for 1 minute**.
- Above 2,000 m altitude, boil for **3 minutes**.
- Let it cool covered. To improve the taste, pour it back and forth between containers a few times (adds oxygen).

> Source: CDC — Making Water Safe in an Emergency. https://www.cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/index.html

### Household bleach / hypochlorite (chlorine)

Use only bleach that is **unscented, without color-safe bleach and without additives**, within its expiry date (chlorine loses strength with time and heat).

| Product | Dose per liter of clear water | Waiting time |
|---|---|---|
| Sodium hypochlorite 2.5% (bottle distributed free by Brazil's public health system, SUS) | 2 drops | 30 minutes |
| Common household bleach 2.0–2.5% ("água sanitária" in Brazil) | 2 drops | 30 minutes |
| Bleach 6% (US standard) | 2 drops (8 drops per gallon) | 30 minutes |
| Bleach 8.25% | 1–2 drops (6 drops per gallon) | 30 minutes |

- Cloudy or very cold water: **double the dose** and wait longer.
- After 30 minutes there should be a **slight smell of chlorine**. If there isn't, repeat the dose and wait another 15 minutes.

> Sources: Ministério da Saúde (Brazilian Ministry of Health) — guidance on using 2.5% sodium hypochlorite in water for human consumption; CDC — Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water. https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/emergency-disinfection-drinking-water

### SODIS — solar disinfection

1. Use **clear PET bottles, label removed, up to 2 liters**, without heavy scratches.
2. The water must be clear (you can read large letters through the full bottle).
3. Lay the bottles down in full sun, preferably on a roof tile or metal sheet.
4. **6 hours** of strong sun; **2 consecutive days** if the sky is more than half cloudy.
5. Does not work well in continuous rain.

> Source: Eawag/SANDEC — SODIS Manual. https://www.sodis.ch

### Commercial filters and tablets

- Ceramic or membrane filters (0.1–0.2 micron) remove bacteria and protozoa; most **do not remove viruses**. Combine with chlorine when the water comes from areas with sewage.
- Sodium dichloroisocyanurate (NaDCC) or chlorine dioxide tablets: follow the package instructions.
- Household clay (candle) filters improve water but do not replace boiling/chlorine for high-risk water.

sources.section: Questions to Jared › Why chlorination but no modern and less dangerous technologies to purify water? Especially from boreholes with expected low turbidity? Chlorine is pretty dangerous stuff and the supply change is another hazard as well as special requirements to the equipment. Why not Ultra-Filtration or UV-C treatment?
heading_path: Why chlorination but no modern and less dangerous technologies to purify water? Especially from boreholes with expected low turbidity? Chlorine is pretty dangerous stuff and the supply change is another hazard as well as special requirements to the equipment. Why not Ultra-Filtration or UV-C treatment?
sources.text: Open the full source below. This section is unavailable or too long to include safely as a complete passage.
sources.original_text:
In many (if not most) remote applications, it is advisable to use simple and robust technologies that are easy to operate and maintain. Tablet and flow-activated chlorinators provide this level of functionality for low-turbidity groundwater, where ultrafiltration (UF) and UV disinfection are more sophisticated treatment technologies with higher capital costs and much more significant operational costs and maintenance burdens. In particular, UF and UV are energy-intensive, which in this context would require large solar arrays or standby power facilities.

Chlorine disinfection produces a chlorine residual in the finished water which protects against biological contamination into the distribution system, where UF and UV do not.

Calcium hypochlorite in granular and tablet form is widely available and has a long shelf life. There are safety concerns with handling chlorine, but safety protocols exist and many organizations around the world use chlorine for water treatment safely and effectively. The key to a successful installation, as with any other technology, is the proper training of operators.

sources.text: Open the full source below. This section is unavailable or too long to include safely as a complete passage.
sources.original_text:
Household bleach sold for use in laundering clothes is a 3–8% solution of sodium hypochlorite at the time of manufacture. Strength varies from one formulation to another and gradually decreases with long storage. Sodium hydroxide is usually added in small amounts to household bleach to slow down the decomposition of NaClO.[10]

Domestic use patio blackspot remover products are ~10% solutions of sodium hypochlorite.

A 10–25% solution of sodium hypochlorite is, according to Univar's safety sheet, supplied with synonyms or trade names bleach, Hypo, Everchlor, Chloros, Hispec, Bridos, Bleacol, or Vo-redox 9110.[35]

A 12% solution is widely used in waterworks for the chlorination of water, and a 15% solution is more commonly[36] used for disinfection of wastewater in treatment plants. Sodium hypochlorite can also be used for point-of-use disinfection of drinking water,[37] taking 0.2–2 mg of sodium hypochlorite per liter of water.[38]

Dilute solutions (50 ppm to 1.5%) are found in disinfecting sprays and wipes used on hard surfaces.[39][40]

sources.original_text:
Enabor, B. Integrated Water Management by Urban Poor Women: A Nigerian Slum Experience. Int. J. of Water Resources Development 14, 505-512 (1998).

Abstract:

A study was carried out on the integrated water management in an urban poor community in Ibadan, Nigeria. This community with a population of 20 938 is located in the Koloko-Aiyekalearea under the North East Local Government occupying an area of 0.97 km2. They engage mostly in trading, farming and some have taken up the civil service and teaching professions. Shallow wells are their main water source supplemented by rain, tap and other commercial sources. Sanitation is poor, characterized by spread of wastewater on streets and unkempt open drains, and streets littered with refuse and animal dung. An intervention study covering a period of over 18 months was undertaken involving 324 women to improve the water quality, to lay a hygienic drainage system, and to use the wastewater for backyard or community farming. Simple storage of water for prolonged periods, solar radiation of stored water, and pot chlorination of wells were tried for the improvement of water quality. The merits of these methods were assessed and related to the community's perceptions, knowledge, attitudes and practices. The women formed a ten-member water committee and examined various feasible solutions. Solar radiation for water quality improvement,drainage improvement through digging deeper and periodic cleaning, and community farming using the drainage water were finally adopted and practised. The produce obtained from the farming activities improved their income generation, nutritional needs and general sustainability.

URL: http://www.informaworld.com/openurl?genre=article&doi=10.1080/07900629849132&magic=crossref%7C%7CD404A21C5BB053405B1A640AFFD44AE3

heading_path: Remote Monitoring of Water Treatment Systems in Ethiopia
sources.text: Open the full source below. This section is unavailable or too long to include safely as a complete passage.
sources.original_text:
Background:

Pathogens that carry diseases such as cholera can spread through contaminated drinking water and pose a threat to health. In many regions worldwide, water is available, but water sources are polluted, so it is very important to use water treatment systems. For this reason, it is important to monitor water quality.

Using EcoPhi’s Monitoring System to Ensure Good Water Quality:

EcoPhi is monitoring different water treatment systems in Ethiopia. EcoPhi takes care of the remote monitoring of the water treatment plants and provides a central dashboard for all systems and detailed information about each system. The data from the water treatment system is transmitted to the EcoPhi Box via a UART interface. EcoPhi sends this data to the cloud platform, where it is displayed graphically and where users can access and analyse it. The Advanced Box sends the data via the mobile data network. In the event of connection failures or poor connection, the EcoPhi Box stores the data locally and sends it as soon as the connection is re-established. Critical alarms can also be sent directly from the device via SMS. This allows the systems to be monitored even in remote regions.

How the System Helps the People in Ethiopia:

Through the EcoPhi monitoring system, the partners can check at any time whether the systems are working and whether the dosing unit is functioning properly and the chlorine content is correct. A large number of systems can be monitored through the platform. User-specific displays and specific reports allow the team to focus only on the critical facilities. The service enables insight into the system. When comparing multiple systems, weak points can be identified and corrected. Quick failure analyses can be made, allowing technicians to prepare specifically for them, thereby saving travel time. The specified alarms make it possible to intervene quickly in the event of problems with the systems.

sources.title: Disinfection by-product
sources.text: Open the full source below. This section is unavailable or too long to include safely as a complete passage.
sources.original_text:
Chlorinated disinfection agents such as chlorine and monochloramine are strong oxidizing agents introduced into water in order to destroy pathogenic microbes, to oxidize taste/odor-forming compounds, and to form a disinfectant residual so water can reach the consumer tap safe from microbial contamination. These disinfectants may react with naturally present fulvic and humic acids, amino acids, and other natural organic matter, as well as iodide and bromide ions, to produce a range of DBPs such as the trihalomethanes (THMs), haloacetic acids (HAAs), bromate, and chlorite (which are regulated in the US), and so-called "emerging" DBPs such as halonitromethanes, haloacetonitriles, haloamides, halofuranones, iodo-acids such as iodoacetic acid, iodo-THMs (iodotrihalomethanes), nitrosamines, and others.[1]

Chloramine has become a popular disinfectant in the US, and it has been found to produce N-nitrosodimethylamine (NDMA), which is a possible human carcinogen, as well as highly genotoxic iodinated DBPs, such as iodoacetic acid, when iodide is present in source waters.[1][2]

Residual chlorine and other disinfectants may also react further within the distribution network – both by further reactions with dissolved natural organic matter and with biofilms present in the pipes. In addition to being highly influenced by the types of organic and inorganic matter in the source water, the different species and concentrations of DBPs vary according to the type of disinfectant used, the dose of disinfectant, the concentration of natural organic matter and bromide/iodide, the time since dosing (i.e. water age), temperature, and pH of the water.[3]

Swimming pools using chlorine have been found to contain trihalomethanes, although generally they are below current EU standard for drinking water (100 micrograms per litre).[4] Concentrations of trihalomethanes (mainly chloroform) of up to 0.43 ppm have been measured.[5] In addition, trichloramine has been detected in the air above swimming pools,[6] and it is suspected in the increased asthma observed in elite swimmers. Trichloramine is formed by the reaction of urea (from urine and sweat) with chlorine and gives the indoor swimming pool its distinctive odor.

**NO.** Do not cut the wound, do not try to suck out the venom, and do **not** tie a tight tourniquet. These actions can cause severe tissue damage, accelerate venom spread, or lead to shock [S1], [S7].

Since you are alone with no phone service, follow these steps immediately:

1.  **Move Away Safely:** If the snake is still nearby, move away quickly without looking down at your foot. Do not try to catch or kill the snake; a photo from a distance (if safe) can help later [S7].
2.  **Stop Movement Immediately:** Keep the bitten ankle completely still. Walking accelerates venom effects and makes transport harder [S1], [S2].
3.  **Remove Tight Items:** Take off rings, bracelets, shoes, or socks from that leg before any swelling occurs [S1], [S7].
4.  **Signal for Help:** Use a whistle, light, or mirror to signal nearby people. Ask anyone who reaches you to summon rescue and arrange transport [S3].
5.  **Wait if Possible:** If you cannot move safely or do not know a safe route, stay in a safe place and keep signaling. There is no universal "safe walking distance" after a bite [S3].
6.  **If You Must Move:** Only walk toward help as your last option if the route is known and safe. Walk with minimal exertion to slow venom spread [S3].
7.  **Clean Gently (Optional):** If available, wash the area with soap and water, but do not delay movement for this step [S4], [S7]. *(Note: Australian guidelines advise against cleaning as traces of venom may help identify the species later).*
8.  **Stay Calm:** Reassure yourself; panic increases heart rate and spreads venom faster [S1].

**Warning Signs:** Monitor your breathing closely while waiting for help. Watch for worsening swelling, difficulty breathing, or feeling faint. If you feel your vision blurring or you become confused, try to signal even harder immediately [S1], [S2].

**Professional Help Required:** Antivenom is the only effective treatment for snakebite envenoming [S7]. You must be transported urgently to a referral hospital once help arrives [S7]. This advice does not replace professional medical care.

sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.text: It may be difficult to determine if a bite by any species of snake is life-threatening. A bite by a North American copperhead on the ankle is usually a moderate injury to a healthy adult, but a bite to a child's abdomen or face by the same snake may be fatal. The outcome of all snakebites depends on a multitude of factors: the type of snake, the size, physical condition, and temperature of the snake, the age and physical condition of the person, the area and tissue bitten (e.g., foot, torso, vein or muscle), the amount of venom injected, the time it takes for the person to find treatment, and finally the quality of that treatment.[2][49] An overview of systematic reviews on different aspects of snakebite management found that the evidence base from majority of treatment modalities is low quality.[50] An analysis of World Health Organization guidelines found that they are of low quality, with inadequate stakeholder involvement and poor methodological rigour.[51] In addition, access to effective treatment modalities is a major challenge in some regions, particularly in most African countries.[52]

The following treatments, while once recommended, are considered of no use or harmful, including tourniquets, incisions, suction, application of cold, and application of electricity.[58] Cases in which these treatments appear to work may be the result of dry bites.

- Application of a tourniquet to the bitten limb is generally not recommended. There is no convincing evidence that it is an effective first-aid tool as ordinarily applied.[67] Tourniquets have been found to be completely ineffective in the treatment of Crotalus durissus bites,[68] but some positive results have been seen with properly applied tourniquets for cobra venom in the Philippines.[69] Uninformed tourniquet use is dangerous since reducing or cutting off circulation can lead to gangrene, which can be fatal.[67] The use of a compression bandage is generally as effective, and much safer.
- Cutting open the bitten area, an action often taken before suction, is not recommended since it causes further damage and increases the risk of infection; the subsequent cauterization of the area with fire or silver nitrate (also known as infernal stone) is also potentially threatening.[70]
- Sucking out venom, either by mouth or with a pump, does not work and may harm the affected area directly.[71] Suction started after three minutes removes a clinically insignificant quantity—less than one-thousandth of the venom injected—as shown in a human study.[72] In a study with pigs, suction not only caused no improvement but led to necrosis in the suctioned area.[73] Suctioning by mouth presents a risk of further poisoning through the mouth's mucous tissues.[74] The helper may also release bacteria into the person's wound, leading to infection.
- Immersion in warm water or sour milk, followed by the application of snake-stones (also known as la Pierre Noire), which are believed to draw off the poison in much the way a sponge soaks up water.
- Application of a one-percent solution of potassium permanganate or chromic acid to the cut, exposed area.[70] The latter substance is notably toxic and carcinogenic.
- Drinking abundant quantities of alcohol following the cauterization or disinfection of the wound area.[70]
- Use of electroshock therapy in animal tests has shown this treatment to be useless and potentially dangerous.[75][76][77][78]

In extreme cases, in remote areas, all of these misguided attempts at treatment have resulted in injuries far worse than an otherwise mild to moderate snakebite. In worst-case scenarios, thoroughly constricting tourniquets have been applied to bitten limbs, completely shutting off blood flow to the area. By the time the person finally reached appropriate medical facilities, their limbs had to be amputated.

**Do:**
- Move away from the snake; don't try to catch it (a photo from a distance helps with identification).
- Keep the victim **calm, lying down and with the limb still**.
- Remove rings, bracelets and shoes (the limb may swell).
- Wash the area with soap and water.
- Take them urgently to a referral hospital: **antivenom is the only effective treatment**.
- Offer water if conscious.

**DO NOT:** apply a tourniquet or tight band, cut, suck, burn, apply herbs, kerosene, alcohol, coffee grounds or any substance to the bite, or give alcoholic drinks.

**DO NOT INSERT AN IV.**

Based on the provided safety guidelines, inserting an IV (intravenous line) is a procedure that must be left to trained practitioners. Attempting this without training can cause severe infection, nerve damage, or worsen the patient's condition.

**Immediate Actions:**
1.  **Call emergency services** immediately if possible.
2.  **Focus on stopping the bleeding** using direct pressure.
3.  **Do not attempt** any invasive procedures like IV insertion, suturing deep wounds, or resetting bones.

### How to Stop the Bleeding (Thigh)
Since the bleeding is from the thigh (a limb), follow these steps for life-threatening external bleeding [S1], [S2], [S3]:

**Step 1: Apply Firm Direct Pressure**
*   Press firmly and continuously on the wound with a clean cloth, gauze, or your own hand (if wearing a glove or plastic) [S1].
*   Maintain this pressure until bleeding stops or help takes over [S2].
*   **Do not remove** the cloth if it soaks through; instead, put more cloth on top and keep pressing [S1].

**Step 2: Apply a Tourniquet (If Direct Pressure Fails)**
If the bleeding is life-threatening and does not stop with direct pressure, use a tourniquet. You do **not** need an IV kit for this; a wide strip of cloth (3–5 cm) and a stick to twist can work as an improvised tourniquet [S1].

*   **Placement:** Place the tourniquet **5–7 cm above the wound** toward the heart, ensuring it is **not over a joint** [S1], [S3]. For the thigh, place it high on the upper leg if you are unsure of the exact wound location ("high and tight") [S1].
*   **Tighten:** Tighten the tourniquet (using the stick to twist) until the bleeding **stops completely** [S1], [S3]. It will hurt; this is normal [S1].
*   **Secure:** Secure it tightly so it does not loosen. Do **not** loosen or remove the tourniquet once applied [S1], [S3].
*   **Record Time:** Write down the exact time the tourniquet was applied on the person's forehead or directly on the tourniquet [S1].

**Step 3: Manage Shock and Positioning**
*   Lay the person down and keep them warm to prevent shock [S1].
*   If signs of shock appear (pale skin, rapid breathing), keep the person flat on their back unless they have a suspected head, neck, or back injury, in which case keep them still [S6].

**Important Warnings:**
*   **No IVs:** Leave invasive vein access to trained practitioners. Do not attempt to insert an IV [S2].
*   **Internal Bleeding Warning:** Heavy bleeding from the thigh can sometimes indicate internal injury or a major artery rupture (like a femoral artery bleed). Definitive treatment often requires rapid surgery. If the person shows signs of severe shock (confusion, unconsciousness), professional help is critical [S6].
*   **Infection Risk:** Do not close dirty wounds. Keep the area clean if possible, but stopping the bleeding takes priority [S7].

**Summary:** Stop the bleeding with pressure and a tourniquet. Do not touch the IV kit. Wait for medical professionals.

Main article:

Emergency bleeding control §

Wound management

For the long process of regeneration of the body tissues, see

Wound healing

and

Wound bed preparation

.

Acute bleeding from an injury to the skin is often treated by the application of direct pressure.[9] For severely injured patients, tourniquets are helpful in preventing complications of shock.[10] Anticoagulant medications may need to be discontinued and possibly reversed in patients with clinically significant bleeding.[11] Patients that have lost excessive amounts of blood may require a blood transfusion.[12]

The use of cyanoacrylate glue to prevent bleeding and seal battle wounds was designed and first used in the Vietnam War.[13] Skin glue, a medical version of "super glue", is sometimes used instead of using traditional stitches used for small wounds that need to be closed at the skin level.[14]

sources.text:
Emergency bleeding control

Emergency bleeding control
Specialty | Emergency medicine

Emergency bleeding control describes actions that control bleeding from a patient who has suffered a traumatic injury or who has a medical condition that has caused bleeding. Many bleeding control techniques are taught as part of first aid throughout the world.[1] Other advanced techniques, such as tourniquets, are taught in advanced first aid courses and are used by health professionals to prevent blood loss by arterial bleeding.[2] To manage bleeding effectively, it is important to be able to readily identify types of wounds and types of bleeding.

sources.title: Emergency bleeding control
sources.text:
Internal wounds (usually to the torso) are harder to deal with than external wounds, although they often have an external cause. The key dangers of internal bleeding include hypovolaemic shock (leading to exsanguination), a tamponade on the heart or a haemothorax on the lung. The aortic aneurysm is a special case where the aorta, the body's main blood vessel, becomes ruptured through an inherent weakness, although exertion, raised blood pressure or sudden movements could cause a sudden catastrophic failure.[23] This is one of the most serious medical emergencies a patient can face, as the only treatment is rapid surgery.

Calling emergency medical services is required for internal bleeding.

Generally, the person should stay in the same position if a head, neck or back injury is suspected (unless either moving is required for safety reasons or to control bleeding).[24]

If signs and symptoms of shock are encountered, the person should be positioned flat on the back (unless the person prefers otherwise for confort and breathing).[24]

Treatment of internal bleeding is beyond the scope of simple first aid, and a person giving first aid should consider it potentially life-threatening. The definitive treatment for internal bleeding is always surgical treatment, and medical advice must be sought urgently for any victim of internal bleeding.[25]

sources.text:
1. Wash your hands. Control the bleeding.
2. **Irrigate the wound with plenty of drinking water** (boiled and cooled, or treated): use a syringe or a plastic bag with a hole to make a jet. Washing well is more important than antiseptic.
3. Remove visible dirt with clean (boiled) tweezers.
4. Clean, recent (< 6–8 hours) and superficial wounds can be closed with adhesive strips ("steri-strip" type or tape cut into a butterfly shape).
5. **Do not close** dirty wounds, puncture wounds, animal/human bites or old wounds: clean them, cover with a clean moist dressing and change it daily.
6. Tetanus: keep your vaccination up to date **before** the crisis (booster every 10 years).

**Signs of infection:** spreading redness, warmth, swelling, increasing pain, pus, bad smell, red streaks running up the limb, fever. A spreading infection is a medical emergency — antibiotics only with professional guidance.

> Source: Werner, D. — *Onde Não Há Médico* (*Where There Is No Doctor*) (Hesperian Health Guides), chapter on wounds. https://hesperian.org ; WHO — *Best Practice Guidelines on Emergency Surgical Care in Disaster Situations*.

- Suspect a fracture if there is severe pain, deformity, swelling, inability to move or bear weight.
- **Immobilize** in the position found, including the joint above and below the injury, with an improvised splint (sticks, cardboard, rolled-up magazines) and strips of cloth. Pad it.
- Check circulation below the splint (color, temperature, sensation) and loosen it if it turns purple or numb.
- **Open fracture:** control the bleeding without pressing on the bone, cover with a clean damp cloth, do not push the bone back in; high risk of infection — seek medical care.
- **Suspected spinal injury** (fall from height, diving, accident): don't move the person unless necessary; keep head and neck aligned.
- Sprain: rest, ice wrapped in cloth (20 min every 2–3 h), light compression and elevation.

> Source: IFRC 2020; Werner, D. — *Onde Não Há Médico* (*Where There Is No Doctor*).

1. **Is the scene safe?** Don't become a second victim (fire, electricity, traffic, collapse).
2. **Responsive?** Tap the shoulders and call out loudly.
3. **X — eXsanguinating hemorrhage:** severe bleeding? Control it first (see below).
4. **A — airway:** open? Tilt the head and lift the chin (if there is no suspected neck injury).
5. **B — breathing:** look, listen and feel for up to 10 seconds. No breathing or only "gasps" (gasping) = cardiac arrest → CPR.
6. **C — circulation:** pallor, cold and clammy skin, rapid pulse = shock.
7. **D — level of consciousness (disability).**
8. **E — exposure:** look for other injuries and protect from the cold.

**Recovery position:** an unconscious person who is breathing normally, with no suspected spinal injury, should be placed on their side so they don't choke on vomit.

> Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) — *International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020*.

- Suspect a fracture if there is severe pain, deformity, swelling, inability to move or bear weight.
- **Immobilize** in the position found, including the joint above and below the injury, with an improvised splint (sticks, cardboard, rolled-up magazines) and strips of cloth. Pad it.
- Check circulation below the splint (color, temperature, sensation) and loosen it if it turns purple or numb.
- **Open fracture:** control the bleeding without pressing on the bone, cover with a clean damp cloth, do not push the bone back in; high risk of infection — seek medical care.
- **Suspected spinal injury** (fall from height, diving, accident): don't move the person unless necessary; keep head and neck aligned.
- Sprain: rest, ice wrapped in cloth (20 min every 2–3 h), light compression and elevation.

> Source: IFRC 2020; Werner, D. — *Onde Não Há Médico* (*Where There Is No Doctor*).

1. **Is the scene safe?** Don't become a second victim (fire, electricity, traffic, collapse).
2. **Responsive?** Tap the shoulders and call out loudly.
3. **X — eXsanguinating hemorrhage:** severe bleeding? Control it first (see below).
4. **A — airway:** open? Tilt the head and lift the chin (if there is no suspected neck injury).
5. **B — breathing:** look, listen and feel for up to 10 seconds. No breathing or only "gasps" (gasping) = cardiac arrest → CPR.
6. **C — circulation:** pallor, cold and clammy skin, rapid pulse = shock.
7. **D — level of consciousness (disability).**
8. **E — exposure:** look for other injuries and protect from the cold.

**Recovery position:** an unconscious person who is breathing normally, with no suspected spinal injury, should be placed on their side so they don't choke on vomit.

> Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) — *International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020*.

**Ação Imediata e Segurança**
1. **Afaste-se da área:** Não tente capturar a cobra ou perseguí-la; uma foto à distância (se possível) ajuda na identificação futura [S1].
2. **Minimize movimentos:** Mantenha-se imóvel e reduza o esforço físico para retardar a circulação do veneno, especialmente se a picada for grave [S3].
3. **Verifique sinais vitais:** Observe sua respiração; se houver dificuldade ou parar, inicie RCP imediatamente (apenas se estiver inconsciente e com ausência de respiração) [S1][S2].

**Como Sinalizar para a Ajuda (Está sozinho)**
4. **Use recursos sonoros ou visuais:** Se tiver apito, luz ou espelho, use-os para chamar atenção de pessoas próximas ou equipes de resgate [S3].
5. **Escolha o local seguro:** Fique em um local seguro e continue sinalizando; não tente caminhar até a ajuda se não houver uma rota conhecida e segura [S3].
6. **Aguarde com calma:** Não há tempo universalmente seguro para esperar; fique imóvel enquanto a ajuda chega [S3].

**Cuidados Locais e Proibições (Sem fontes específicas para esta situação de "sem sinal", aplicam-se princípios gerais de segurança)**
*   **Lave o local:** Se houver água disponível, lave a picada com água e sabão. Algumas organizações recomendam isso para remover veneno residual na pele [S4]. *Nota: Recomendações variam por região; se não houver água, não tente limpar agressivamente.*
*   **Remova restrições:** Tire anéis, pulseiras ou calçados que possam apertar devido ao inchaço [S1].
*   **NÃO faça o seguinte (Perigo de morte):**
    *   Não aplique torniquete nem garrote (causa gangrena e amputação) [S6].
    *   Não corte, sugue o veneno ou queime a área [S6].
    *   Não aplique ervas, querosene, álcool ou pó de café no local [S1][S6].
    *   Não dê bebida alcoólica se estiver sozinho (impossível) e nem se houver companheiros [S1].

**Transporte Urgente**
7. **Busque transporte assim que possível:** Assim que alguém chegar, peça para levá-lo imediatamente em uma maca (carregue deitado) até um hospital de referência; caminhar deve ser feito apenas como última opção e com mínimo esforço [S2][S3].
8. **Informe o médico:** Leve qualquer foto da cobra ou descrição do local para ajudar na escolha do soro antiveneno correto [S4].

**Sem apoio de fontes locais (Conhecimento Geral sobre Picadas de Cobra)**
*   **Identificação do Veneno:** O resultado depende muito da espécie, tamanho da cobra, local da picada e quantidade de veneno injetado. Uma picada na perna pode ser moderada para um adulto saudável, mas fatal para uma criança ou se atingir o abdômen [S5].
*   **Tratamento Definitivo:** O soro antiveneno é o único tratamento eficaz conhecido; primeiros socorros são apenas temporários [S1][S4].
*   **Risco de Amputação:** Tentativas caseiras erradas (como torniquetes muito apertados) podem destruir a perna, exigindo amputação antes mesmo de chegar ao hospital [S6].

**Alerta de Saúde e Segurança**
*   **Procure ajuda profissional imediatamente:** A orientação não substitui um médico. O atraso no tratamento é o maior fator de risco para morte ou sequelas graves [S5].
*   **Monitoramento:** Fique atento a sinais de choque (pele pálida/fria, tontura, dificuldade respiratória) enquanto espera o resgate.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text: It may be difficult to determine if a bite by any species of snake is life-threatening. A bite by a North American copperhead on the ankle is usually a moderate injury to a healthy adult, but a bite to a child's abdomen or face by the same snake may be fatal. The outcome of all snakebites depends on a multitude of factors: the type of snake, the size, physical condition, and temperature of the snake, the age and physical condition of the person, the area and tissue bitten (e.g., foot, torso, vein or muscle), the amount of venom injected, the time it takes for the person to find treatment, and finally the quality of that treatment.[2][49] An overview of systematic reviews on different aspects of snakebite management found that the evidence base from majority of treatment modalities is low quality.[50] An analysis of World Health Organization guidelines found that they are of low quality, with inadequate stakeholder involvement and poor methodological rigour.[51] In addition, access to effective treatment modalities is a major challenge in some regions, particularly in most African countries.[52]

sources.text:
Old-style snake bite kit that should not be used

The following treatments, while once recommended, are considered of no use or harmful, including tourniquets, incisions, suction, application of cold, and application of electricity.[58] Cases in which these treatments appear to work may be the result of dry bites.

- Application of a tourniquet to the bitten limb is generally not recommended. There is no convincing evidence that it is an effective first-aid tool as ordinarily applied.[67] Tourniquets have been found to be completely ineffective in the treatment of Crotalus durissus bites,[68] but some positive results have been seen with properly applied tourniquets for cobra venom in the Philippines.[69] Uninformed tourniquet use is dangerous since reducing or cutting off circulation can lead to gangrene, which can be fatal.[67] The use of a compression bandage is generally as effective, and much safer.
- Cutting open the bitten area, an action often taken before suction, is not recommended since it causes further damage and increases the risk of infection; the subsequent cauterization of the area with fire or silver nitrate (also known as infernal stone) is also potentially threatening.[70]
- Sucking out venom, either by mouth or with a pump, does not work and may harm the affected area directly.[71] Suction started after three minutes removes a clinically insignificant quantity—less than one-thousandth of the venom injected—as shown in a human study.[72] In a study with pigs, suction not only caused no improvement but led to necrosis in the suctioned area.[73] Suctioning by mouth presents a risk of further poisoning through the mouth's mucous tissues.[74] The helper may also release bacteria into the person's wound, leading to infection.
- Immersion in warm water or sour milk, followed by the application of snake-stones (also known as la Pierre Noire), which are believed to draw off the poison in much the way a sponge soaks up water.
- Application of a one-percent solution of potassium permanganate or chromic acid to the cut, exposed area.[70] The latter substance is notably toxic and carcinogenic.
- Drinking abundant quantities of alcohol following the cauterization or disinfection of the wound area.[70]
- Use of electroshock therapy in animal tests has shown this treatment to be useless and potentially dangerous.[75][76][77][78]

In extreme cases, in remote areas, all of these misguided attempts at treatment have resulted in injuries far worse than an otherwise mild to moderate snakebite. In worst-case scenarios, thoroughly constricting tourniquets have been applied to bitten limbs, completely shutting off blood flow to the area. By the time the person finally reached appropriate medical facilities, their limbs had to be amputated.

sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text: Abra a fonte completa abaixo. Esta seção está indisponível ou é longa demais para ser incluída na íntegra.
sources.original_text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Old-style snake bite kit that should not be used

The following treatments, while once recommended, are considered of no use or harmful, including tourniquets, incisions, suction, application of cold, and application of electricity.[58] Cases in which these treatments appear to work may be the result of dry bites.

- Application of a tourniquet to the bitten limb is generally not recommended. There is no convincing evidence that it is an effective first-aid tool as ordinarily applied.[67] Tourniquets have been found to be completely ineffective in the treatment of Crotalus durissus bites,[68] but some positive results have been seen with properly applied tourniquets for cobra venom in the Philippines.[69] Uninformed tourniquet use is dangerous since reducing or cutting off circulation can lead to gangrene, which can be fatal.[67] The use of a compression bandage is generally as effective, and much safer.
- Cutting open the bitten area, an action often taken before suction, is not recommended since it causes further damage and increases the risk of infection; the subsequent cauterization of the area with fire or silver nitrate (also known as infernal stone) is also potentially threatening.[70]
- Sucking out venom, either by mouth or with a pump, does not work and may harm the affected area directly.[71] Suction started after three minutes removes a clinically insignificant quantity—less than one-thousandth of the venom injected—as shown in a human study.[72] In a study with pigs, suction not only caused no improvement but led to necrosis in the suctioned area.[73] Suctioning by mouth presents a risk of further poisoning through the mouth's mucous tissues.[74] The helper may also release bacteria into the person's wound, leading to infection.
- Immersion in warm water or sour milk, followed by the application of snake-stones (also known as la Pierre Noire), which are believed to draw off the poison in much the way a sponge soaks up water.
- Application of a one-percent solution of potassium permanganate or chromic acid to the cut, exposed area.[70] The latter substance is notably toxic and carcinogenic.
- Drinking abundant quantities of alcohol following the cauterization or disinfection of the wound area.[70]
- Use of electroshock therapy in animal tests has shown this treatment to be useless and potentially dangerous.[75][76][77][78]

In extreme cases, in remote areas, all of these misguided attempts at treatment have resulted in injuries far worse than an otherwise mild to moderate snakebite. In worst-case scenarios, thoroughly constricting tourniquets have been applied to bitten limbs, completely shutting off blood flow to the area. By the time the person finally reached appropriate medical facilities, their limbs had to be amputated.

sources.doc_title: WHO — Snakebite first aid and transport
sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text: Abra a fonte completa abaixo. Esta seção está indisponível ou é longa demais para ser incluída na íntegra.
sources.original_text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

**SITUACIÓN CRÍTICA:** Mordedura de serpiente + Solo + Sin señal.

**1. PRIORIDAD INMEDIATA: SEGURIDAD Y MOVIMIENTO**
*   **No camine a menos que sea estrictamente necesario.** El movimiento acelera la diseminación del veneno por el sistema linfático [S2].
*   Si está herido y no puede moverse con seguridad, **quédese en un lugar seguro** (protegido de elementos y depredadores) y espere a que llegue la ayuda. No existe una distancia o tiempo de espera universalmente seguro tras una mordedura [S3].
*   Si su única opción para sobrevivir es llegar a una ruta conocida o ayuda visible, camine con el **mínimo esfuerzo posible** hacia allí [S3].

**2. SEÑALIZAR PARA OBTENER AYUDA (Sin teléfono)**
*   Utilice cualquier recurso disponible para alertar:
    *   Silbato (sonido repetitivo).
    *   Llama una luz potente o encienda un fuego seguro (si hay combustible y no hay riesgo de incendio forestal inminente).
    *   Use un espejo para reflejar la luz solar hacia puntos distantes [S3].
*   Si alguien llega, pídales que avisen inmediatamente a los servicios de rescate locales [S3].

**3. TRATAMIENTO DE PRIMEROS AUXILIOS (HAGA)**
*   **Manténgase INMÓVIL:** Acuéstese o siéntese sin mover la pierna mordida. Esto es vital para reducir la velocidad del veneno [S1][S2].
*   **Retire objetos apretados:** Quite anillos, pulseras y calzado de esa pierna inmediatamente por si hay hinchazón [S1].
*   **Lave suavemente:** Limpie el área con agua y jabón (si está disponible) para reducir carga bacteriana [S1][S4].
*   **Hidratación:** Beba agua lentamente si está consciente y puede tragar. No tome alcohol ni bebidas energéticas [S1].
*   **Identifique la serpiente (seguro):** Si pudo verlo sin acercarse, intente tomar una foto desde lejos o recuerde su color/patrón para que el personal médico sepa qué antiveneno usar [S1][S4].

**4. LO QUE NO DEBE HACER (NO HAGA)**
*   **NUNCA aplique torniquetes** ni ligaduras apretadas. Son ineficaces y causan gangrena o amputación [S6].
*   **NUNCA corte, sude o succionar** la herida (con boca o bomba). No extrae veneno útil y puede causar infección o necrosis [S6][S7].
*   **NUNCA aplique frío, electricidad, hierbas, queroseno o alcohol** en la herida [S1][S6].

**5. CUÁNDO BUSCAR AYUDA PROFESIONAL (CRÍTICO)**
*   **Todo caso de mordedura de serpiente requiere atención médica urgente.** Solo el antiveno (suero) es el tratamiento eficaz; los remedios caseros no funcionan y pueden dañar más [S1][S5].
*   Los resultados dependen de múltiples factores: tipo de serpiente, cantidad de veneno, edad del paciente y rapidez del tratamiento [S5].
*   Si la hinchazón se extiende rápidamente, aparecen manchas oscuras en la piel, dificultad para respirar o confusión mental, busque ayuda inmediata al menor tiempo posible [S1][S5].

> **Nota sobre el transporte:** Si llega alguien, pida que use una camilla para trasladarlo. Hacer caminar a la víctima puede empeorar la situación [S2].

**Sin respaldo de fuentes locales:**
*   Mantenga la calma; el pánico aumenta el ritmo cardíaco y la circulación del veneno.
*   Cubra la herida con un vendaje limpio y seco (no apretado) solo para protegerla de suciedad, a menos que las guías locales específicas para esa región indiquen lo contrario.

sources.text:
**Haga:**
- Aléjese de la serpiente; no intente capturarla (una foto a distancia ayuda a identificarla).
- Mantenga a la víctima **tranquila, acostada y con el miembro inmóvil**.
- Retire anillos, pulseras y calzado (el miembro puede hincharse).
- Lave el lugar con agua y jabón.
- Llévela con urgencia a un hospital de referencia: **el suero antiofídico (antiveneno) es el único tratamiento eficaz**.
- Ofrezca agua si está consciente.

**NO haga:** torniquete o ligadura, cortes, succión, quemar, aplicar hierbas, queroseno, alcohol, café molido ni ninguna sustancia en el lugar, ni dar bebidas alcohólicas.

> Fuente: Ministério da Saúde (Brasil) — Acidentes por animais peçonhentos: o que fazer e como evitar. https://www.gov.br/saude/pt-br/assuntos/saude-de-a-a-z/a/animais-peconhentos

sources.text: Si está solo sin señal de teléfono tras una mordedura de serpiente, señale a personas cercanas con silbato, luz o espejo, si dispone de ellos. Pida a quien llegue que avise al rescate y ayude a organizar el traslado. Minimice el movimiento mientras la ayuda pueda llegar hasta usted. Si ir hasta la ayuda es su única opción, y puede hacerlo con seguridad por una ruta conocida, camine hacia la ayuda con el mínimo esfuerzo posible. Si no puede moverse con seguridad o no conoce una ruta segura, permanezca en un lugar seguro y siga señalando. No existe una distancia de caminata ni un tiempo de espera universalmente seguro tras una mordedura.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text: It may be difficult to determine if a bite by any species of snake is life-threatening. A bite by a North American copperhead on the ankle is usually a moderate injury to a healthy adult, but a bite to a child's abdomen or face by the same snake may be fatal. The outcome of all snakebites depends on a multitude of factors: the type of snake, the size, physical condition, and temperature of the snake, the age and physical condition of the person, the area and tissue bitten (e.g., foot, torso, vein or muscle), the amount of venom injected, the time it takes for the person to find treatment, and finally the quality of that treatment.[2][49] An overview of systematic reviews on different aspects of snakebite management found that the evidence base from majority of treatment modalities is low quality.[50] An analysis of World Health Organization guidelines found that they are of low quality, with inadequate stakeholder involvement and poor methodological rigour.[51] In addition, access to effective treatment modalities is a major challenge in some regions, particularly in most African countries.[52]

sources.text:
Old-style snake bite kit that should not be used

The following treatments, while once recommended, are considered of no use or harmful, including tourniquets, incisions, suction, application of cold, and application of electricity.[58] Cases in which these treatments appear to work may be the result of dry bites.

- Application of a tourniquet to the bitten limb is generally not recommended. There is no convincing evidence that it is an effective first-aid tool as ordinarily applied.[67] Tourniquets have been found to be completely ineffective in the treatment of Crotalus durissus bites,[68] but some positive results have been seen with properly applied tourniquets for cobra venom in the Philippines.[69] Uninformed tourniquet use is dangerous since reducing or cutting off circulation can lead to gangrene, which can be fatal.[67] The use of a compression bandage is generally as effective, and much safer.
- Cutting open the bitten area, an action often taken before suction, is not recommended since it causes further damage and increases the risk of infection; the subsequent cauterization of the area with fire or silver nitrate (also known as infernal stone) is also potentially threatening.[70]
- Sucking out venom, either by mouth or with a pump, does not work and may harm the affected area directly.[71] Suction started after three minutes removes a clinically insignificant quantity—less than one-thousandth of the venom injected—as shown in a human study.[72] In a study with pigs, suction not only caused no improvement but led to necrosis in the suctioned area.[73] Suctioning by mouth presents a risk of further poisoning through the mouth's mucous tissues.[74] The helper may also release bacteria into the person's wound, leading to infection.
- Immersion in warm water or sour milk, followed by the application of snake-stones (also known as la Pierre Noire), which are believed to draw off the poison in much the way a sponge soaks up water.
- Application of a one-percent solution of potassium permanganate or chromic acid to the cut, exposed area.[70] The latter substance is notably toxic and carcinogenic.
- Drinking abundant quantities of alcohol following the cauterization or disinfection of the wound area.[70]
- Use of electroshock therapy in animal tests has shown this treatment to be useless and potentially dangerous.[75][76][77][78]

In extreme cases, in remote areas, all of these misguided attempts at treatment have resulted in injuries far worse than an otherwise mild to moderate snakebite. In worst-case scenarios, thoroughly constricting tourniquets have been applied to bitten limbs, completely shutting off blood flow to the area. By the time the person finally reached appropriate medical facilities, their limbs had to be amputated.

sources.doc_title: WHO — Snakebite first aid and transport
sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text: Abra la fuente completa abajo. Esta sección no está disponible o es demasiado larga para incluirla completa.
sources.original_text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

### Ação Imediata para Hemorragia com Risco de Vida

1.  **Chame a emergência** imediatamente. O tempo é crítico em sangramentos arteriais ou graves [S2].
2.  **Aplique o torniquete comercial** na coxa:
    *   Posicione-o **5–7,5 cm acima da ferida**, em direção ao coração (na raiz do membro), nunca sobre uma articulação como o joelho [S3].
    *   Aperte a alavanca (windlass) até que o sangramento **pare completamente** [S3].
    *   **Fixe** o torniquete e **anote a hora** de aplicação (na própria pessoa ou no dispositivo) [S4][S3].
3.  **Mantenha pressão direta firme** sobre a ferida com gaze ou pano limpo até que chegue ajuda profissional, mesmo após aplicar o torniquete, se possível [S2].
4.  **NÃO afrouxe nem remova o torniquete**. Deixe isso exclusivamente para profissionais de saúde no atendimento médico [S3].
5.  **Deixe a pessoa aquecida** e em posição confortável (deitada), monitorando-a até a chegada da ajuda [S1][S7].

### Sem apoio de fontes locais: Instruções Específicas sobre o Kit de Acesso IV

*   **NÃO utilize o kit de acesso IV.** A inserção de cateteres venosos é um procedimento invasivo que exige treinamento especializado. Tentar fazer isso sem qualificação pode causar infecções graves, danos aos vasos sanguíneos ou piorar a situação do paciente [S2].
*   O uso de torniquetes comerciais foi desenhado para ser aplicado por leigos em emergências de vida ou morte quando a pressão direta não basta [S3].
*   Se o torniquete comercial estiver disponível, ele é a ferramenta correta e segura para controlar sangramentos graves em membros [S3].

**⚠️ Sinais de Alerta:**
Se a pessoa ficar inconsciente, não respirar ou tiver pulso ausente após o controle do sangramento, inicie RCP (Reanimação Cardiovascular) imediatamente enquanto aguarda ajuda. A orientação fornecida não substitui o atendimento médico profissional.

sources.doc_title: Primeiros socorros e cuidados de saúde
sources.text:
1. **Pressão direta firme** sobre a ferida com pano limpo, gaze ou a própria mão (com luva ou plástico) por pelo menos 10 minutos, sem aliviar para "olhar".
2. Se encharcar, **não retire**: coloque mais pano por cima e continue pressionando.
3. Ferida profunda (axila, virilha, pescoço): **encha a ferida (tamponamento)** com gaze/pano limpo, empurrando para dentro, e mantenha pressão forte.
4. **Torniquete** — para sangramento com risco de vida em braço ou perna que não para com pressão:
   - Coloque **5–7 cm acima da ferida** (nunca sobre a articulação); se não souber onde é, coloque "alto e apertado" na raiz do membro.
   - Aperte até o sangramento **parar**. Dói — é normal.
   - **Anote a hora** (na testa ou no torniquete). Não afrouxe; leve a pessoa a atendimento.
   - Improvisado: faixa larga (3–5 cm) + bastão para girar (molinete). Corda fina e arame cortam a pele e não funcionam bem.
5. Deite a pessoa, mantenha-a aquecida (prevenção do choque).

> Fonte: American College of Surgeons — *Stop the Bleed*. https://www.stopthebleed.org ; IFRC 2020.

sources.title: Bleeding
sources.text:
Main article:

Emergency bleeding control §

Wound management

For the long process of regeneration of the body tissues, see

Wound healing

and

Wound bed preparation

.

Acute bleeding from an injury to the skin is often treated by the application of direct pressure.[9] For severely injured patients, tourniquets are helpful in preventing complications of shock.[10] Anticoagulant medications may need to be discontinued and possibly reversed in patients with clinically significant bleeding.[11] Patients that have lost excessive amounts of blood may require a blood transfusion.[12]

The use of cyanoacrylate glue to prevent bleeding and seal battle wounds was designed and first used in the Vietnam War.[13] Skin glue, a medical version of "super glue", is sometimes used instead of using traditional stitches used for small wounds that need to be closed at the skin level.[14]

sources.title: Emergency bleeding control
sources.text:
Emergency bleeding control

Emergency bleeding control
Specialty | Emergency medicine

Emergency bleeding control describes actions that control bleeding from a patient who has suffered a traumatic injury or who has a medical condition that has caused bleeding. Many bleeding control techniques are taught as part of first aid throughout the world.[1] Other advanced techniques, such as tourniquets, are taught in advanced first aid courses and are used by health professionals to prevent blood loss by arterial bleeding.[2] To manage bleeding effectively, it is important to be able to readily identify types of wounds and types of bleeding.

sources.title: Emergency bleeding control
sources.text:
Main article:

Emergency tourniquet

Another method of achieving constriction of the supplying artery is a tourniquet - a band tied tightly around a limb to restrict blood flow. Tourniquets are routinely used to bring veins to the surface for cannulation, though their use in emergency medicine is more limited. Many armies carry a tourniquet as part of their personal first aid kit.

Improvised tourniquets, in addition to creating potential problems for the ongoing medical management of the patient, usually fail to achieve force enough to adequately compress the arteries of the limb. As a result, they not only fail to stop arterial bleeding, but may actually increase bleeding by impairing venous bloodflow.[16]

sources.doc_title: Primeiros socorros e cuidados de saúde
sources.text:
1. **Cena segura?** Não vire uma segunda vítima (fogo, eletricidade, trânsito, desabamento).
2. **Responde?** Toque nos ombros e chame em voz alta.
3. **X — hemorragia eXsanguinante:** sangramento grave? Controle primeiro (veja abaixo).
4. **A — vias aéreas:** abertas? Incline a cabeça e eleve o queixo (se não houver suspeita de trauma de pescoço).
5. **B — respiração:** olhe, ouça e sinta por até 10 segundos. Respiração ausente ou só "suspiros" (gasping) = parada cardíaca → RCP.
6. **C — circulação:** palidez, pele fria e úmida, pulso rápido = choque.
7. **D — nível de consciência.**
8. **E — exposição:** procure outras lesões e proteja do frio.

Para sangramento externo intenso, chame a emergência [S2]. Pressione a ferida com firmeza e continuamente com gaze ou pano limpo [S2]. Mantenha a pressão até parar ou chegar ajuda [S2]. Mantenha pressão firme enquanto obtém um torniquete comercial para hemorragia com risco de vida num membro; siga as instruções separadas do torniquete [S2]. Fique com a pessoa [S2]. Se não tiver treinamento, não insira um acesso IV; deixe o acesso invasivo à veia para profissionais treinados [S2].

Para hemorragia com risco de vida num braço ou perna, use um torniquete comercial se disponível, seguindo suas instruções [S3]. Coloque-o 5–7,5 cm acima da ferida em direção ao coração, nunca sobre uma articulação [S3]. Aperte até parar o sangramento e fixe [S3]. Não afrouxe nem retire [S3]. Chame a emergência; mantenha pressão direta firme enquanto obtém o torniquete ou se não houver um disponível [S3]. O treinamento é ideal, mas não atrase cuidados vitais esperando uma pessoa treinada [S3].

sources.text:
1. **Pressão direta firme** sobre a ferida com pano limpo, gaze ou a própria mão (com luva ou plástico) por pelo menos 10 minutos, sem aliviar para "olhar".
2. Se encharcar, **não retire**: coloque mais pano por cima e continue pressionando.
3. Ferida profunda (axila, virilha, pescoço): **encha a ferida (tamponamento)** com gaze/pano limpo, empurrando para dentro, e mantenha pressão forte.
4. **Torniquete** — para sangramento com risco de vida em braço ou perna que não para com pressão:
   - Coloque **5–7 cm acima da ferida** (nunca sobre a articulação); se não souber onde é, coloque "alto e apertado" na raiz do membro.
   - Aperte até o sangramento **parar**. Dói — é normal.
   - **Anote a hora** (na testa ou no torniquete). Não afrouxe; leve a pessoa a atendimento.
   - Improvisado: faixa larga (3–5 cm) + bastão para girar (molinete). Corda fina e arame cortam a pele e não funcionam bem.
5. Deite a pessoa, mantenha-a aquecida (prevenção do choque).

> Fonte: American College of Surgeons — *Stop the Bleed*. https://www.stopthebleed.org ; IFRC 2020.

sources.title: Bleeding
sources.text:
Main article:

Emergency bleeding control §

Wound management

For the long process of regeneration of the body tissues, see

Wound healing

and

Wound bed preparation

.

Acute bleeding from an injury to the skin is often treated by the application of direct pressure.[9] For severely injured patients, tourniquets are helpful in preventing complications of shock.[10] Anticoagulant medications may need to be discontinued and possibly reversed in patients with clinically significant bleeding.[11] Patients that have lost excessive amounts of blood may require a blood transfusion.[12]

The use of cyanoacrylate glue to prevent bleeding and seal battle wounds was designed and first used in the Vietnam War.[13] Skin glue, a medical version of "super glue", is sometimes used instead of using traditional stitches used for small wounds that need to be closed at the skin level.[14]

sources.title: Emergency bleeding control
sources.text:
Emergency bleeding control

Emergency bleeding control
Specialty | Emergency medicine

Emergency bleeding control describes actions that control bleeding from a patient who has suffered a traumatic injury or who has a medical condition that has caused bleeding. Many bleeding control techniques are taught as part of first aid throughout the world.[1] Other advanced techniques, such as tourniquets, are taught in advanced first aid courses and are used by health professionals to prevent blood loss by arterial bleeding.[2] To manage bleeding effectively, it is important to be able to readily identify types of wounds and types of bleeding.

sources.title: Emergency bleeding control
sources.text:
Main article:

Emergency tourniquet

Another method of achieving constriction of the supplying artery is a tourniquet - a band tied tightly around a limb to restrict blood flow. Tourniquets are routinely used to bring veins to the surface for cannulation, though their use in emergency medicine is more limited. Many armies carry a tourniquet as part of their personal first aid kit.

Improvised tourniquets, in addition to creating potential problems for the ongoing medical management of the patient, usually fail to achieve force enough to adequately compress the arteries of the limb. As a result, they not only fail to stop arterial bleeding, but may actually increase bleeding by impairing venous bloodflow.[16]

validation_inputs.draft:
⚠️ **Prioridad de Seguridad:** El sangrado abundante en el muslo es una emergencia vital que puede causar shock hemorrágico y muerte en minutos. Actúe inmediatamente siguiendo la prioridad: **Controlar la hemorragia antes que cualquier otra cosa**.

### 1. Aplicación del Torniquete Comercial (Prioridad Máxima)
Dado que hay un torniquete comercial disponible, este es el método más efectivo para controlar hemorragias de extremidades superiores a una articulación [S2].

**Pasos exactos:**
1.  **Coloque el torniquete:** Posicione la banda sobre la piel sana, **2-3 cm por encima del sitio de la herida** (más alto en dirección al corazón). Si la herida está justo debajo de la cadera o cerca de la articulación, colóquelo lo más alto posible en el muslo [S2].
    *   *Nota:* No lo coloque sobre una articulación ni directamente sobre la ropa.
2.  **Apriete hasta detener el flujo:** Use la herramienta de apriete (la tuerca o palanca) para girarla y tensar la banda. Debe ejercer suficiente fuerza para que el sangrado se detenga por completo.
3.  **Verifique:** Si la sangre sigue saliendo, apriete más hasta que sea un flujo cero.
4.  **Fije la herramienta:** Una vez detenido el sangrado, asegure firmemente la tuerca/palanca para que no se afloje accidentalmente.
5.  **Anote la hora:** Escriba la hora exacta de aplicación en la frente o mejilla de la persona y anótela también si hay alguien con usted. Esto es crucial para el personal médico posterior [S2].

### 2. Uso del Equipo IV (Solo como medida complementaria)
El equipo IV **no detiene** el sangrado activo por sí solo; su función es reponer líquidos una vez que la hemorragia está controlada o mientras se estabiliza al paciente.
*   **Condición crítica:** Solo intente insertar un catéter IV si ya ha colocado el torniquete y el flujo sanguíneo ha cesado, o si hay personal entrenado disponible para ello. Insertar IVs en personas con shock hemorrágico no controlado es ineficaz sin detener la pérdida de sangre primero [S2].
*   **Acción:** Si logra insertar una vía, colóquela lo más proximal posible (más cerca del cuerpo) y administre solución salina lentamente mientras espera ayuda médica. No intente administrar medicamentos ni fluidos en grandes cantidades sin indicación médica clara.

### 3. Señales de Alarma y Ayuda Profesional
Busque asistencia médica profesional inmediatamente después de controlar la hemorragia. Este escenario requiere hospitalización urgente.

**Señales de alarma (Shock Hemorrágico):**
*   La persona se desmaya o pierde el conocimiento.
*   Piel fría, húmeda y pálida (o azulada en labios).
*   Respiración muy rápida y superficial.
*   Pulso débil o difícil de sentir.
*   Confusión extrema o agitación.

**Acciones finales:**
1.  **No quite el torniquete:** Nunca retire un torniquete comercial antes de que llegue personal médico entrenado, incluso si la herida parece haber cicatrizado o sangrado [S2].
2.  **Mantenga a la persona tumbada:** Coloque a la víctima acostada sobre su espalda (posiblemente con las piernas ligeramente elevadas si no hay fracturas) para mejorar el retorno venoso.
3.  **Envíe ayuda:** Llame al número de emergencia local (112, 911, etc.) o envíe a alguien por refuerzos. Indique claramente: "Hemorragia controlada con torniquete a las [HORA]".

> Fuente: WHO — *Psychological First Aid: Guide for Field Workers* (2011); IASC — *Guidelines on Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in Emergency Settings* (2007).
> Fuente: US Army ATP 3-50.21 *Survival* (2018), cap. sobre señalización; Convenio de Aviación Civil Internacional (OACI/ICAO), Anexo 12 — señales visuales tierra-aire.

**Nota importante:** Esta información es para situaciones de emergencia offline y no reemplaza la formación médica profesional ni el consejo médico.

sources.section: La mente es el equipo principal
sources.text:
En las crisis largas, el desánimo, el pánico y los conflictos matan tanto como el hambre. Los sobrevivientes suelen tener en común: **calma, rutina, propósito y vínculos**.

### Técnica STOP (cuando aparezca el pánico)

- **S**iéntese (deténgase).
- **T**ranquilícese (respiración lenta: inhale 4 segundos, retenga 4, exhale 6).
- **O**bserve (qué hay alrededor, qué tengo, qué necesito).
- **P**lanifique (un próximo paso simple y concreto).

### Rutina y propósito

- Horarios fijos para despertarse, comer, trabajar, descansar y dormir.
- Tareas para todos, incluidos niños y adultos mayores (todos se sienten útiles).
- Pequeñas metas diarias y celebración cuando se cumplen.
- Momentos de ocio: música, historias, juegos, lectura, oración o meditación según las creencias de cada uno.
- Sueño: 7–9 horas para los adultos siempre que sea posible; túrnense en las guardias.

### Niños

- Mantenga la rutina y explique la situación con palabras simples y verdaderas.
- Los juegos y los dibujos ayudan a procesar el miedo.
- Deles pequeñas responsabilidades (regar la huerta, cuidar a los animales).

### Duelo y trauma

- Permita que las personas hablen (o se queden en silencio) sin forzarlas.
- **Primeros auxilios psicológicos:** observar, escuchar y conectar — ofrecer consuelo, ayudar con las necesidades básicas y vincular a la persona con el apoyo de familiares y de la comunidad.
- Atención a las señales de riesgo: hablar de dejar de vivir, aislamiento total, dejar de comer o de cuidarse. Quédese cerca, no deje sola a la persona y busque apoyo. En Brasil, el CVV (Centro de Valorização da Vida, línea de prevención del suicidio) atiende en el 188 (cuando haya teléfono); en otros países, use la línea de crisis local o el número de emergencias (112 en la Unión Europea, 911 en gran parte de América).

> Fuente: WHO — *Psychological First Aid: Guide for Field Workers* (2011); IASC — *Guidelines on Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in Emergency Settings* (2007).
sources.original_text:
En las crisis largas, el desánimo, el pánico y los conflictos matan tanto como el hambre. Los sobrevivientes suelen tener en común: **calma, rutina, propósito y vínculos**.

### Técnica STOP (cuando aparezca el pánico)

- **S**iéntese (deténgase).
- **T**ranquilícese (respiración lenta: inhale 4 segundos, retenga 4, exhale 6).
- **O**bserve (qué hay alrededor, qué tengo, qué necesito).
- **P**lanifique (un próximo paso simple y concreto).

### Rutina y propósito

- Horarios fijos para despertarse, comer, trabajar, descansar y dormir.
- Tareas para todos, incluidos niños y adultos mayores (todos se sienten útiles).
- Pequeñas metas diarias y celebración cuando se cumplen.
- Momentos de ocio: música, historias, juegos, lectura, oración o meditación según las creencias de cada uno.
- Sueño: 7–9 horas para los adultos siempre que sea posible; túrnense en las guardias.

### Niños

- Mantenga la rutina y explique la situación con palabras simples y verdaderas.
- Los juegos y los dibujos ayudan a procesar el miedo.
- Deles pequeñas responsabilidades (regar la huerta, cuidar a los animales).

### Duelo y trauma

- Permita que las personas hablen (o se queden en silencio) sin forzarlas.
- **Primeros auxilios psicológicos:** observar, escuchar y conectar — ofrecer consuelo, ayudar con las necesidades básicas y vincular a la persona con el apoyo de familiares y de la comunidad.
- Atención a las señales de riesgo: hablar de dejar de vivir, aislamiento total, dejar de comer o de cuidarse. Quédese cerca, no deje sola a la persona y busque apoyo. En Brasil, el CVV (Centro de Valorização da Vida, línea de prevención del suicidio) atiende en el 188 (cuando haya teléfono); en otros países, use la línea de crisis local o el número de emergencias (112 en la Unión Europea, 911 en gran parte de América).

> Fuente: WHO — *Psychological First Aid: Guide for Field Workers* (2011); IASC — *Guidelines on Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in Emergency Settings* (2007).

- **Uso continuo:** reserva de los medicamentos de quienes tienen enfermedades crónicas (presión, diabetes, tiroides, epilepsia, asma) — hable con el médico antes de la crisis sobre recetas para tener reserva.
- **Básicos:** analgésicos/antipiréticos (paracetamol, dipirona/metamizol, ibuprofeno), antialérgico, sales de rehidratación oral, zinc infantil, antiácido, pomada para rozaduras del pañal.
- **Curaciones:** gasa, compresas, vendas elásticas (de crepé), cinta adhesiva/micropore, tiras de aproximación, curitas/tiritas, guantes desechables, solución salina (suero fisiológico), clorhexidina o yodopovidona, tijeras, pinzas, termómetro, torniquete comercial (tipo CAT), vendaje compresivo, manta térmica.
- **Prevención:** protector solar, repelente, mosquiteros, cepillo e hilo dental, toallas sanitarias/copa menstrual, preservativos.
- **Libros impresos recomendados:** *Donde no hay doctor*, *Donde no hay dentista* y *Where Women Have No Doctor* (Hesperian — PDF gratuitos en hesperian.org).

Revise los vencimientos cada 6 meses. Los medicamentos vencidos pierden eficacia; las tetraciclinas vencidas pueden ser tóxicas — no las use.

- **Tres de cualquier cosa** = auxilio: tres fogatas en triángulo, tres silbatazos, tres disparos, tres destellos.
- **SOS** en código Morse: `··· — — — ···` (3 cortos, 3 largos, 3 cortos), con luz o sonido.
- **Espejo de señales:** visible a decenas de kilómetros en un día de sol. Haga una "V" con los dedos extendidos apuntando al objetivo y mueva el reflejo dentro de la V.
- **Señales en el suelo** para aeronaves (grandes, de 3 m o más, contrastantes): **V** = necesito ayuda; **X** = necesito asistencia médica; **flecha** = seguimos en esta dirección.
- **Humo:** de día, humo oscuro (caucho, aceite) sobre fondo claro; o blanco (hojas verdes) sobre el fondo oscuro del bosque.
- Un silbato se oye mucho más lejos que la voz y gasta menos energía.

> Fuente: US Army ATP 3-50.21 *Survival* (2018), cap. sobre señalización; Convenio de Aviación Civil Internacional (OACI/ICAO), Anexo 12 — señales visuales tierra-aire.
